segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: i'd like to begin in a cheap restaurant off a californian freeway, where a guy called jensen and two pals are plotting. they want to take movie quality graphics and cram them into a domestic computer, and their business model, which made people laugh, was games.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: skipping on a decade and a bit, because they did fine in gaming. the turning point is when they opened up the graphics card for everybody. usually a processor's like one brilliant chef cooking course after course. this is ten thousand line cooks each chopping one carrot. cuda was how you shouted orders at them, and anyone could, gratis.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: it took six years for someone to shout the right order. twenty twelve, a canadian grad student trains a neural network on two cards he could have bought on the high street, and beats the world's best image software by over ten points. that is year zero for modern ai. everything since, chatbots and all, has been sitting on those tools.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: so the obvious thing to wonder is how they've hung on to it. and there's not one answer, there's four, piled up like a cake. a rival who matches one slice is still three short, and that's what makes it the benchmark.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: i'm going to begin with the one that i think matters most, which is the software. developers are loyal to what works, and this works out of the box, the way apple stuff does. a thousand plus libraries. nearly twenty years of refinement. and whenever there's some new technique in a paper, the code that comes with it runs on cuda, and the rocm crowd wait months.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: and that's why the hardware itself, which i would normally have started with, isn't the decider. here's the chip comparison. the amd part is cheaper, and it's got nearly a hundred gigabytes more memory than nvidia's workhorse. you'd expect them to be neck and neck. but look at the takings from data centres, a hundred and ninety four billion plays seventeen. twelve dollars for every one.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: you might say fine, amd's too small, what about the really rich ones. google has spent tens of billions over eleven years and they're the best of the rest. the other three hyperscalers are designing their own as well. all of them, and i mean all, are still writing cheques to nvidia.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: i'll stop there. they've got the silicon, the code, the cabling and the factory slots, with every major company and both of the world's heavyweights building on top of it. it only ends if innovation ends. panshul's up next to see if the figures back me up.

segments.speaker: Panshul
segments.say: good afternoon. i want you to just look at this one number for a moment. that came in over one quarter. it finished on the twenty fifth of october and it's a preliminary number, so it may still be adjusted by a small amount.

segments.speaker: Panshul
segments.say: the analysts who follow this for their living, their average guess is the grey. the green is what came in. and you go along, and you go along, and green is above grey thirteen times out of thirteen. so even the optimists were not optimistic enough.

segments.speaker: Panshul
segments.say: i will go directly to what we believe it is worth. we modelled the free cash for five years and discounted using a conservative number from bloomberg. then three cases, good, central, and one where ai budgets pause for some time. in the chart you are seeing the value of one share in each case.

segments.speaker: Mi'kael
segments.say: thanks. so, responsible investing. i won't dodge it, the boss quit less than a fortnight ago. the finance chief's minding the shop on an interim basis, the board's finally got a chair of its own, and there are reports of inquiries by the s e c and by california. that is the g in e s g and it's the weakest letter right now.

segments.speaker: Mi'kael
segments.say: next is the planet, and i want to lead with the ugly number instead of the pretty one. almost all of the carbon footprint comes from suppliers. it's baked in when tsmc and the rest of them fabricate the parts. it's called scope three and look at the direction it's heading. sell more, make more, emit more.

segments.speaker: Mi'kael
segments.say: what they do deserve credit for is their own patch. offices, labs, the computers that they run themselves. in fiscal eighteen about a third of that power was green, and now the whole lot is, a hundred percent. it's a smaller piece of the pie than the suppliers, but it's the piece they can control, and they fixed it.
